title: Are online gig spoilers ruining live music?
description:
Film and TV show spoilers often come with a warning because people know they can be annoying. But when it comes to footage from concerts and gigs… those rules don’t really apply, as Olivia Rodrigo fans found out when clips of a surprise moment from her ‘Unraveled Tour’ went viral on socials.

You might have saved up for a ticket to see your favourite artist, found the perfect outfit and be counting down the days to the big show, but the chances are that you’ll know what’s going to happen way before you get there. Fan clips of all the biggest moments, the surprises and the special guests are usually shared everywhere online and difficult to avoid. If you’ve been to a concert recently, you might have found it irritating if people are filming huge chunks of the show in front of you. Some artists like Phoebe Bridgers, are even banning phones from their concerts.

We ask if gig spoilers ruin the surprise or actually add to the excitement. And, if they’re not for you, what can you do to avoid them when you’re online? We speak to BBC journalist Riyah Collins who has been looking into this and ask music fans from Nigeria, Australia and the UK what they think.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討演唱會短片在社群媒體流傳後，是否會破壞現場演出的驚喜。 BBC 記者 Riyah Collins 以 Olivia Rodrigo 舞臺上的服裝變換為例，說明有些歌迷期待保留第一次觀看的完整體驗，也有人認為短片能增加期待、提供穿搭靈感，讓無法買票或到場的人參與。節目介紹透過取消追蹤歌迷帳號、調整推薦內容或靜音特定主題來減少暴雷的方法，也討論部分藝人限制手機與錄影的做法。受訪者指出，手機可能影響現場的連結感，但網路分享也能擴大演出的可及性；親自到場與線上觀看各有不同價值。
summaryEn: This episode asks whether concert clips shared online spoil the excitement of live music. BBC journalist Riyah Collins discusses a surprise costume change on Olivia Rodrigo's tour and the different reactions it prompted. Some fans want to experience surprises for the first time at their own show, while others find clips exciting, useful for outfit inspiration, or valuable when they cannot afford tickets or attend in person. The programme explores avoiding spoilers by unfollowing fan accounts, changing recommendations, and muting topics. It also considers artists restricting phones or recording, including the use of special phone pouches. The discussion weighs the connection and spontaneity of a live performance against the wider access that online sharing can offer.
